content: Clindesse Vaginal Cream is indicated for the treatment of bacterial vaginosis. It is administered as a single dose by inserting one full applicator intravaginally in non-pregnant patients. Cleocin Vaginal Cream is also used for bacterial vaginosis. In non-pregnant patients, one full applicator is inserted intravaginally at bedtime for either 3 or 7 consecutive days. In pregnant patients, the treatment duration is 7 consecutive days. Cleocin Vaginal Ovules are administered by inserting one suppository into the vagina at bedtime for 3 consecutive days. Xaciato is a vaginal gel containing 100 mg of clindamycin per 5 g of gel. It is administered as a single dose by inserting one applicatorful intravaginally. Bacterial vaginosis, previously referred to as Haemophilus vaginitis, Gardnerella vaginitis, nonspecific vaginitis, Corynebacterium vaginitis, or anaerobic vaginosis, is treated with these medications in females aged 12 years and older. The safety and efficacy of these treatments have not been established in females under 12 years of age. Adverse effects associated with clindamycin use include the following: Body as a whole: Upper respiratory infections. Dermatologic: Pruritic rash, pruritus, and erythema. Gastrointestinal: Diarrhea and vomiting. General: Fatigue. Immune system: Hypersensitivity reactions. Nervous system: Dizziness. Reproductive system: Dysfunctional uterine bleeding, dysuria, dysmenorrhea, intermenstrual bleeding, menorrhagia, pelvic pain, vaginal burning, vaginal irritation, vulvar erythema, vulvitis, vulvovaginal discomfort or pain, vulvovaginal dryness, and vulvovaginitis. Serious adverse effects include pseudomembranous colitis and drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS). Hypersensitivity to clindamycin or other lincosamides is a contraindication. Patients with regional enteritis, ulcerative colitis, or a history of Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea should avoid clindamycin use. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including clindamycin. The severity can range from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, ongoing antibiotic use not directed against C. difficile should be discontinued. Management includes fluid and electrolyte replacement, protein supplementation, and appropriate antibiotic treatment for C. difficile. Barrier contraceptives, such as condoms and diaphragms, should not be used concurrently with or for 5 days following treatment with clindamycin vaginal creams or suppositories. These products contain mineral oil or oleaginous bases that may weaken latex or rubber products. Other clindamycin vaginal products have been used to treat pregnant females during the second and third trimesters. However, clindamycin vaginal phosphate has not been studied in pregnant females. It is unknown whether clindamycin is excreted in human breast milk following vaginal administration, though it has been detected in breast milk after oral or intravenous administration. Clindamycin has the potential to affect the gastrointestinal flora of breastfed infants. Clindamycin is a lincosamide antibacterial agent that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit of susceptible bacteria, interfering with peptide chain initiation. Clindamycin phosphate is inactive in vitro but is converted in vivo through hydrolysis to the active form, clindamycin. For vaginal use only, administration at bedtime is recommended to minimize leakage.
